newsitem.title: CHINA: China says to endorse U.N. social rights covenant.
newsitem.headline: China says to endorse U.N. social rights covenant.

text.p: China, a focus of controversy over its human rights record, said it will sign the U.N. International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights but was silent on a similar pact on political freedoms.

Beijing would sign the covenant before the end of the year and was now studying related domestic legislation, President Jiang Zemin told visiting French Defence Minister Charles Millon in a meeting on Monday.

"We evaluated the International Covenant on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights repeatedly," state media on Tuesday quoted Jiang as saying.
However, Jiang only said China would sign the first of the two covenants and made no further reference to the second.

Diplomats said Beijing's decision to sign the social rights covenant could help China in its fight to avoid international censure on its human rights record, but its choice not to accede to the political pact showed it still had far to go.
"Many countries have been urging the Chinese...to sign up to both of these covenants, and it's encouraging to see them doing one," one diplomat said.
"It will have to be taken into account by governments when they consider their attitude towards China's human rights record."

Denmark on Monday said it would press ahead with a motion to censure China for human rights abuses at the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva despite warnings from Beijing that such a move could damage ties.

Under the social rights pact, Beijing would agree to protect its people from discrimination and ensure fair distribution of natural resources, and would have to submit an annual report to the United Nations on social rights, diplomats said.
"But that's a step along the way, not the end of the story," the diplomat said.
Jiang hailed Beijing's efforts to ensure subsistence for its 1.2 billion people and said China had made great progress in boosting the rule of law to protect civil and political rights.
"The Chinese people in fact enjoy comprehensive human rights," he was quoted as saying.
In its annual human rights report for 1996, the U.S. State Department said China had effectively silenced public dissent by jailing or exiling virtually every active dissident.

Jiang praised Paris for its "wise and far-sighted" decision not to co-sponsor the U.N. resolution criticising Beijing's rights record and said he hoped France would help persuade more Western nations to avoid confrontation in favour of dialogue.
"There is no wonder that there are disputes, but what is more important is the way these disputes are resolved," he was quoted as saying.
The U.N. human rights motion is assured of the backing of the United States and most European Union states, with the notable exceptions of France and Germany.

Previous resolutions to condemn Beijing for its failure to protect fundamental freedoms after its bloody 1989 crackdown on student demonstrators in Tiananmen Square have failed. Each year China has rallied enough support to block the move.
